column4: Moses sees a fire and promises his family a burning brand "لَعَلَّكُمْ تَصْطَلُونَ" so they may warm themselves; the verb directly realizes the section's dictionary scene اصطليت بالنار of a shared household fire.

Moses asks his family to wait while he seeks news or a firebrand "لَعَلَّكُمْ تَصْطَلُونَ"; this repeats the section's exact secondary sense of ص ل و, warming oneself at a fire rather than burning in punishment.

Charity is taken from wealth and the Prophet is told to pray for the givers, for "إِنَّ صَلَاتَكَ سَكَنٌ لَّهُمْ"; the two roots the section joins, prayer ص ل و and repose س ك ن, here meet through giving rather than withholding.
The condemned person "وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ"; its wording exactly repeats 107:3 and supplies the stated cause immediately after his consignment to the fire in 69:31.
The command "ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ" uses the same ص ل و letters as الْمُصَلِّينَ in the section, now unambiguously for making the prisoner enter and endure Hell.
Those who consume orphans' property eat fire into their bellies and "سَيَصْلَوْنَ سَعِيرًا"; abuse of the vulnerable turns food itself into the fire carried by the section's prayer-root.
The people of Saqar answer "لَمْ نَكُ مِنَ الْمُصَلِّينَ"; prayer is named inside the fire interrogation whose next answer is failure to feed the poor.
The next confession is "وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ"; it directly places refusal to feed the poor beside prayer and Saqar, the conjunction developed by the section.
The prisoners add that they denied the Day of Judgment; this completes in Saqar the same chain as surah 107: denial of the dīn, failed prayer, and neglect of the poor.
سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ uses the named root in its punitive fire sense and introduces the very fire in which 74:43-46 connect prayer, poor-feeding, and denial.
The human being becomes "مَنُوعًا" when good reaches him; this is the same withholding root as وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ, immediately before the exception made for the prayerful.
إِلَّا الْمُصَلِّينَ makes true prayer the explicit exception to withholding, reversing the section's الْمُصَلِّينَ who refuse ordinary aid.
These prayerful people are constant in their prayer, a precise reversal of those who are heedless of their prayer in 107:5.
True worshippers have a recognized right in their wealth; this makes material sharing an internal mark of prayer rather than an optional addition to it.
That recognized share belongs to the asker and the deprived, specifying the recipients whose exclusion exposes the section's false worshippers.
وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ is the plural counterpart of 107:3 and locates failure to urge poor-feeding amid greed and the coming of Hell.
The downward course begins with the person who is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient; this gives the moral starting point for the blazing fire later named in 92:14-15.
God's warning "فَأَنْذَرْتُكُمْ نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ" explicitly announces the blaze toward which the miser's course leads.
لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى uses ص ل و for entering and enduring the blaze, the fire-bearing face heard beside الْمُصَلِّينَ in the section.
The one who burns is identified as the person who denied and turned away, joining fire to the opening denial of surah 107.
The Godfearing person gives his wealth to purify himself and is kept from the blaze; generosity is the direct counter-course to the miser of 92:8 and the withholders of the section.
وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ joins the section's disaster cry وَيْل to deniers before their burning is stated in 83:16.
The deniers are those who deny the Day of Judgment, exactly identifying the denial named at the opening of surah 107.
ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ لَصَالُو الْجَحِيمِ carries the named ص ل و root in its fire sense and fulfills the earlier وَيْل against the deniers.
The burning deniers are told that this is what they used to deny, making the punishment answer their earlier stance in its own words.
The paired command to throw every stubborn ingrate into Hell stages the final exposure to fire immediately before the withholding epithet in 50:25.
مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ names the condemned as a persistent preventer of good, the same social action as refusing the small aid of 107:7.
النَّارِ ذَاتِ الْوَقُودِ presents a fire supplied with fuel, exactly one dictionary object of the section's صلاء, but here the fuelled hearth is an instrument of persecution.
The trench-makers sit around the fuelled fire, "إِذْ هُمْ عَلَيْهَا قُعُودٌ"; it is the section's social hearth scene reversed into people calmly watching others burn.
Hoarders of gold and silver who do not spend in God's path are warned of painful punishment; the withheld store becomes the material heated in the next ayah.
The hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs; what was withheld becomes both furnace-work and torment.
Hell's drink is like molten metal "يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ"; the section's dictionary example of roasting meat is grimly transferred to human faces.
God will "نُصْلِيهِمْ نَارًا" and replace their skins whenever they are cooked through; the ayah unites the root's burning sense with the section's roasting image.
The hypocrites rise lazily to prayer "يُرَاءُونَ النَّاسَ" and remember God little; it directly explains the showy, inattentive prayer named in 107:5-6.
Their contributions are rejected because they disbelieve, come to prayer lazily, and spend unwillingly; failed worship and failed giving are diagnosed together.
وَوَيْلٌ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ sounds the same disaster cry as 107:4, and the next ayah defines its targets through refusal of zakāh and denial of the afterlife.
Those under the وَيْل neither give zakāh nor believe in the Hereafter, tightly joining withheld material due with the denial that opens surah 107.
Deniers are violently pushed "إِلَىٰ نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا"; the exact pushing verb used of the orphan in 107:2 is returned upon them at the fire.
They are told, "هَٰذِهِ النَّارُ الَّتِي كُنْتُمْ بِهَا تُكَذِّبُونَ"; the fire is explicitly identified as the reality their denial rejected.
The recipient of the record behind his back will call for destruction, supplying a disaster cry immediately before ص ل و names his burning.
وَيَصْلَىٰ سَعِيرًا places the named root's fire sense directly after the condemned person's cry for ruin, the same sound-structure the section hears in وَيْل and الْمُصَلِّينَ.
وَيْلٌ لِكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُمَزَةٍ begins another sequence in which the woe-cry falls upon a selfish accumulator and ends in a kindled fire.
The target gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it; the hoarded good supplies the social shape behind the fire announced later in the surah.
The hoarder will be thrown into the Crusher, turning private accumulation into forcible exposure to punishment.
The Crusher is identified as "نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ", a deliberately kindled fire that converts the section's useful hearth into judgment.
سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ uses the named root for burning in a flame, while the following ayah supplies the firewood image.
The fire-bound man's wife is "حَمَّالَةَ الْحَطَبِ", a carrier of firewood; the section's fuel sense becomes part of the punitive household pair.
Receiving the record in the left hand prompts the wish that it had never been given; this begins the precise judgment sequence that reaches seizure and burning.
خُذُوهُ فَغُلُّوهُ commands seizure and shackling, the first action in the staged movement completed by the fire command in 69:31.
The first stated cause is failure to believe in God the Great; paired with 69:34, it reproduces surah 107's inseparable denial and social neglect.
The steep path includes feeding on a day of hunger; food shared at the moment of greatest need reverses the withheld hearth of the section.
The first named recipient is an orphan of near kin, answering the orphan who is pushed away in 107:2.
The next recipient is "مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ", a poor person reduced to the dust; the named miskīn is restored to the shared meal.
Those who reject God's signs have a fire closed over them; the passage makes refusal of the steep path of feeding terminate in an enclosing fire.
The rebuke begins with failure to honor the orphan, placing the other vulnerable figure of surah 107 beside the refusal to urge poor-feeding in 89:18.
They consume inheritance voraciously; predatory eating stands beside their refusal to secure food for the poor.
Their immense love of wealth explains why the orphan and poor are excluded and prepares the judgment scene that follows.
Hell is brought forth on that Day after the rebuke for greed and neglected feeding, completing the same movement from an unshared table to fire.
When told to spend from God's provision, the disbelievers refuse to feed those God could have fed; disbelief becomes an argument for withholding food.
مَنَّاعٍ لِلْخَيْرِ repeats 50:25's exact characterization of the habitual preventer of good, clarifying the disposition behind refusing al-māʿūn.
The garden owners resolve that no miskīn shall enter the orchard that day; the poor person is deliberately excluded from available food.
They set out early with firm power to withhold, turning the refusal of a poor person's share into a deliberate collective plan.
When the crop is ruined, the withholders recognize that they themselves have become deprived; exclusion of the poor returns as their own deprivation.
The righteous feed food they love to a miskīn, orphan, and captive; the two vulnerable figures of surah 107 are welcomed to the meal.
They feed solely for God's face and seek neither reward nor thanks, a precise reversal of the visible performance condemned in 107:6.
Expiation includes feeding ten poor people from the average food one feeds one's own family; the domestic table becomes the measure for sharing with the miskīn.
People of means are forbidden to swear off giving to relatives, the poor, and emigrants and are told to pardon; a self-imposed refusal to share is explicitly revoked.
Shuʿayb's people ask whether his prayer commands them to abandon what they please to do with their wealth; even their taunt recognizes that ṣalāt reaches economic conduct.
Later generations neglect prayer and follow desires, then meet ruin; it is a direct Qur'anic counterpart to being heedless of one's prayer.
Prayer is said to restrain indecency and recognized wrong; a prayer compatible with repelling the vulnerable and withholding aid fails this stated function.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans, the poor, travelers, and petitioners, then establishing prayer and zakāh; shared provision and ṣalāt form one integrity.
The covenant joins good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, and the poor with upright speech, prayer, and zakāh; it directly reverses worship severed from vulnerable neighbors.
Charity performed "رِئَاءَ النَّاسِ" is voided by its motive; the same showing-off root exposes why an outward act cannot compensate for a heart closed to others.
Those who spend only to be seen by people and disbelieve in God and the Last Day combine ostentation, material action, and denial exactly as surah 107 diagnoses them.
Abraham says "أَسْكَنْتُ" of settling his family by the Sacred House, then asks that they establish prayer and be provided fruits; dwelling, prayer, and provision meet in one household petition.
The warned fire has people and stones as its fuel; the section's ordinary fuel for a useful hearth is reversed so the unjust become the fuel.
Neither wealth nor children will avail the disbelievers, who are themselves "وَقُودُ النَّارِ"; hoarded means fail and their owners become fuel.
Believers must protect themselves and their households from a fire whose fuel is people and stones; the domestic responsibility of a household is framed against the unshareable final fire.
The hearers are asked to consider the fire they kindle, bringing the ordinary human hearth itself into view.
God asks whether people created the fire's tree or He did, relocating ownership of even the hearth's fuel from the possessive householder to the Provider.
God made kindled fire both a reminder and a benefit for travelers; its warmth and utility are provision to be received, while its reminder points beyond the domestic flame.
Material is heated in fire to make ornaments or useful goods, and its dross rises away; this is the Qur'an's clearest parallel to fire making resistant material fit for a purpose.
Dhu al-Qarnayn heats iron blocks until they are like fire and then pours molten copper over them; controlled heat transforms hard material into a protective structure.
Those who evade the campaign rejoice at staying behind and dislike striving in heat, but are told Hell is fiercer in heat; avoiding present heat does not spare them the heat to be endured.
فَمَا أَصْبَرَهُمْ عَلَى النَّارِ confronts people who traded guidance with what it means to bear fire, closely matching the dictionary sense of enduring an affair's heat and severity.
The Godfearing person is kept far from the blaze; the principal boundary is that giving wealth in 92:18 leads away from the fire that receives the miser.
The hosts prefer others over themselves despite their own need and are saved from inner stinginess; this is the communal home opposite to refusing even small household aid.
Abraham's enemies command one another to burn him, converting communal zeal into a human furnace; the next ayah marks fire's divinely imposed boundary.
God tells the fire to be coolness and safety for Abraham; fire that was meant as torment becomes shelter, sharply separating destructive flame from protective warmth.
God makes human houses "سَكَنًا", places of rest; this primary Qur'anic sense of the poor-person root sets the shared shelter against a home whose implements are withheld.
Abraham quickly brings his guests a roasted calf; the section's cooked-meat hearth appears here as generous hospitality rather than private consumption.
Abraham slips away to his household and brings a fat calf, making the household store serve an unexpected guest.
He places the food before the guests and invites them to eat; the act supplies the open table missing from the section's withheld hearth.
These believers carefully guard their prayers, the direct opposite of being heedless of prayer in 107:5.
Successful believers are humble in their prayer, opposing the prayer performed for display.
The same portrait makes them active in zakāh, so inwardly humble prayer issues in material care.
They guard their prayers, completing the reversal of negligence toward prayer.
True believers establish prayer and spend from what God provided; giving is presented as a coordinate sign of the same faith.
Believing servants are commanded to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly before the irreversible Day, answering both ostentation and withholding.
The humbly fearful establish prayer and spend from God's provision; reverent worship opens the hand rather than closing it.
Trade does not distract these people from remembrance, prayer, or zakāh, and they fear the Day; attentive prayer, giving, and judgment-consciousness answer all three failures of surah 107.
Those who recite God's book establish prayer and spend secretly and openly, hoping in a trade that will not perish; their prayer circulates provision instead of hoarding it.
Those who answer their Lord establish prayer, consult together, and spend from provision; worship is embedded in shared communal action.
Jesus says God enjoined prayer and zakāh upon him throughout life, keeping worship and material duty together.
Ishmael commands his household to prayer and zakāh; the home itself becomes a place where worship and giving are taught together.
The orphan must not be oppressed, a direct reversal of pushing the orphan away in surah 107.
The petitioner must not be repelled, extending the open-handed household stance to the person who asks.
Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring his family a brand or find guidance at it; it is the parallel family-fire scene completed with the warming verb in 27:7 and 28:29.
The Flood's onset is marked when the tannūr erupts; an ordinary oven or hearth becomes the sign that domestic security has given way to judgment.
The repeated Flood account again begins rescue when the tannūr erupts, preserving the striking reversal of the household oven into a catastrophic boundary.
The hypocrites are likened to one who kindles a fire that lights the surroundings before God removes its light; an outwardly successful flame becomes darkness, like outward prayer emptied of care.
The lamp in a niche, glass, and oil almost glowing before fire supply a luminous household fire-image; 24:37 then joins remembrance to prayer and zakāh.
The lamp image is carried into houses where God's name is remembered morning and evening; the next ayah identifies occupants whose prayer and giving survive worldly distraction.
Solomon's workers make large serving basins and fixed cauldrons and are told to work gratefully; abundant household vessels are framed as gifts demanding gratitude, not objects to withhold.
God makes fire for people from the green tree, and they kindle from it; the usable hearth is itself provided rather than privately self-created.
The unjust become firewood for Hell; the domestic fuel named in the section is transformed into the fate of those who deviate.
The condemned are dragged through boiling water and then stoked in the fire, turning the actions of a heated vessel and furnace upon their bodies.
Boiling liquid melts what is inside the condemned and their skins; punitive heat takes on the section's cooking and softening actions.
Whenever they try to leave the anguish they are returned and told to taste the burning punishment; this is forced endurance of heat and severity.
Saqar scorches human skin, specifying the bodily action of the fire introduced with the ص ل و verb in 74:26.
When Hell sees them from afar they hear its fury and roaring; this gives literal fire-sound to the section's claim that the name can be heard with fire in it.
When people are thrown into Hell they hear it inhaling or roaring as it boils, again making punitive fire an audible presence.
Cast bound into a narrow place of the Fire, the condemned call there for destruction; the fire elicits the calamity-cry heard in وَيْل.
They are told not to call for one destruction but for many, intensifying the ruin-cry attached to entering the fire.
After refusing to encourage poor-feeding, the prisoner has no close friend that Day; denied social care returns as complete isolation.
He has no food except foul discharge; the one who would not support the miskīn's food now faces an unshareable anti-meal.
Only sinners eat that food, completing the reversal of wholesome food denied to the poor.
وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ directs the same woe-cry at people whose economic practice takes fully and gives less.
The defrauders demand full measure when receiving from others; their receptive hand is open only toward themselves.
When measuring or weighing for others they cause loss, a commercial counterpart to withholding the small goods another person needs.
Deniers are ordered to proceed toward what they denied; the command begins a fire scene that ends under the refrain of woe.
They are sent to a three-branched shadow, an apparent shelter that the next ayah denies any sheltering power.
The shadow neither shades nor protects from flame; it is the direct opposite of the useful fire and shelter conjoined in the section's domestic hearth.
After the flame throws its sparks, the refrain says woe that Day to the deniers, joining وَيْل, denial, and fire in one unit.
وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ follows their refusal to bow, linking the woe of deniers to a failed bodily act of worship.
The wicked "يَصْلَوْنَهَا يَوْمَ الدِّينِ"; the named root means burning precisely on the Day of Judgment denied in 107:1.
The most wretched enters "النَّارَ الْكُبْرَىٰ" through the ص ل و verb, another direct Qur'anic use of the root's punitive face.
In that fire he neither dies nor lives, sharpening the dictionary sense of having to endure an affair's heat and severity.
Humiliated faces "تَصْلَىٰ نَارًا حَامِيَةً"; the same root states direct exposure to intensely hot fire.
Whoever commits aggression and injustice will be made to enter fire, "فَسَوْفَ نُصْلِيهِ نَارًا"; the root's burning sense is tied to violating others' rights.
The one who breaks with the Messenger and follows another way is consigned to Hell with "نُصْلِهِ جَهَنَّمَ", confirming the root's fire sense.
جَهَنَّمَ يَصْلَوْنَهَا describes those who exchanged God's favor for disbelief entering Hell, another exact burning use of the named root.
The person who wants only the immediate world is assigned Hell "يَصْلَاهَا مَذْمُومًا مَّدْحُورًا"; ص ل و marks the final exposure after self-directed appetite.
God knows best who most deserves "صِلِيًّا" in Hell; the verbal noun preserves the root's sense of exposure to fire.
اصْلَوْهَا الْيَوْمَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ is a direct command to enter the fire because of disbelief, joining the root's fire sense to denial.
Those who follow false gods can mislead only one destined to be "صَالِ الْجَحِيمِ"; the participle shares the section's root in its burning sense.
The transgressors have Hell "يَصْلَوْنَهَا", another direct use of ص ل و for entering and bearing the fire.
وَتَصْلِيَةُ جَحِيمٍ names the hostile reception of a denier as burning in Hell, using the same root as the section's prayer-name.
The opponents' prayer at the House is reduced to whistling and clapping, then they are told to taste punishment for disbelief; empty ritual does not shield from judgment.
The condemned person neither affirmed the truth nor prayed; the next ayah identifies denial and turning away as the paired stance.
وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ repeats the denial-and-turning formula of 92:16 after failure to pray.
Worship of God is joined to good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, the miskīn, neighbors, travelers, and dependents; devotion is tested across the whole household and social circle.
The proud are those who are miserly, command miserliness, and conceal God's bounty; it expands the active withholding condemned in the section.
Those who are miserly and command others to miserliness repeat the section's failure both to give and to urge care.
Some who are called to spend instead withhold, and the ayah says their withholding turns against themselves; the closed hand creates its owner's loss.
Believers are told to listen, obey, and spend, and those guarded from their own stinginess prosper; release from inner withholding is made the condition of success.
The Godfearing assign in their wealth a due for the asker and the deprived, anticipating the explicit recognized share of the prayerful in 70:24-25.
The relative, the miskīn, and the traveler must be given their due; the poor person's claim is treated as a right, not discretionary leftovers.
The relative, miskīn, and traveler are again to receive their due, and such giving is named the path to success.

The detailed household rule permits eating from relatives' and friends' houses and says there is no blame in eating together or separately; the home table is structured for access rather than jealous closure.
Whatever people spend, God replaces, and He is the best provider; fear of depletion is answered by the Provider behind the household store.
God softens iron for David; although fire is not named, the specific softening of rigid material may echo the section's fire-softened stick.
David is told to fashion armor and measure its links; with 34:10, the softened material is deliberately made fit, though the section's straightening-by-fire link remains indirect.
